sentences.text: Rimasuchus possessed a short and broad snout, a shape known as brevirostrine, and could reach lengths of 7 meters or more. Its teeth were robust and blunt, differing from those of other crocodiles, and they were bicarinated, meaning they featured ridges on both the front and back surfaces.
This predator hunted large mammals, including primitive humans.
Evidence of its diet includes tooth marks on Homo habilis fossils, showing bisected bites and perforations typical of crocodile attacks.

Lieutenant Colonel Arthur H. Lloyd collected the first fossil in Wadi Moghara, Egypt, during the early 20th century. Fourtau described the holotype specimen CGM 15597 in 1918 as Crocodylus lloydi, a name that honored the discoverer.
The genus Rimasuchus was eventually named by Storrs in 2003.
As a large semi-terrestrial predator, Rimasuchus likely competed directly with Nile crocodiles.

Fossils found in situ include fish, birds, and mammals such as pigs, elephants, giraffes, bovines, rhinos, and primates. Bone accumulations in beds I and II at Olduvai Gorge have been specifically attributed to Rimasuchus. A trench containing primitive bovine bones, horses, specimen OH 7, and stone tools also held Rimasuchus teeth.
There has been very little study on ontogenetic variation in Rimasuchus and modern crocodiles.

Rimasuchus is now considered more closely related to modern African dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus) than to the genus Crocodylus. It is closely related to the modern dwarf crocodile Osteolaemus and belongs to the group Osteolaeminae. The genus belongs to the parent group Osteolaemini and is classified in the family Crocodylidae. Rimasuchus is a member of the class Reptilia.

Rimasuchus lived during the Early Miocene. Fossils of Rimasuchus date from approximately 1.88 to 7.44 million years ago. The genus Rimasuchus lived from the Burdigalian to the Late Pleistocene, between 20.45 and 0.0117 million years ago.

Rimasuchus fossils have been found in Egypt and possibly Libya. These fossils are found in sandstones and mudstones deposited in lakes and rivers. The earliest Rimasuchus specimens were found in North Africa, but how the species evolved and spread remains uncertain.

Martin Pickford named the Namibian material Crocodylus gariepensis in 2003, suggesting it was the ancestor of the Nile crocodile. It is debated whether some Rimasuchus specimens are actually very large examples of Crocodylus niloticus due to similarities between them.
